I think you two are using different definitions, but the basic design of the gasoline powered engine has not changed much at all baring materials and computer sciences. In 1908 a Ford Model T got 25 mpg. In 2013, the average car got 24.7 mpg according to the EPA. More valves per cylinder, OHC and other improvements have not impacted transportation as dramatically as computer science or atomic theory have impacted the world. The V8 pushrod in a 1969 Camaro is strikingly similar to the computer controlled cylinder selective V8 pushrod in a modern top of the line Corvette and make surprisingly comparable power levels. But a 1969 computer compared to a 2013 smart phone are worlds apart. Granted, materials and transmission gearing have come a long way and allow modern vehicle to move faster, produce more power and carry a heavier load, but they are still limited to stochiometry of ideal gas and air mixtures and volumetric efficiency. I suspect your argument perhaps unknowingly hinges on the fact that the basic chemistry and cylinder layout of a gasoline engine can't change much. Modern automobiles have computer controlled ignitions and fuel sensors, but are comparable to their 100 year old predecessors in several aspects other than of course safety, emissions and top speed. I'd focus on the difference between revolutionary and evolutionary changes. Evolutionary change are things that that enhanced or improve an already existing design. Revolutionary changes are things that entirely replace the existing design with a fundamentally different concept. Going from early flight attempts which basically involved trying to mimic a bird by flapping wings to understanding and applying the concept of lift would be a revolutionary change as the entire concept of how things ought generally work changed. Whereas going from the most basic lift + center of mass thrust aimed model to modern supersonic vessels has just been evolutionary even though the advance in technology has been enormous.

And similarly in engine mechanics there have been enormous evolutionary changes but not real revolutionary changes. The fact you can still refer to them both as internal combustion engines is pretty much a giveaway there. It's all just a semantics issue.

An engine is a large air pump. That hasn't changed.

Engines are now controlled electronically, with thousands of improvements on the model T.

So really it's just semantics and is a stupid argument.

I agree with you, it's the same technology, just vastly improved. There has been some additional technologies that have been added to piston engines in order to improve them, but the engine itself is still an internal combustion engine.

This argument hinges on (most likely) a subtly different definition of "technology." If your opponent regards many adaptations as new technologies then he's right. If you regard few adaptations as new technologies then you're right. I think the issue is a matter of degree and not kind, which is usually subjective.

You might actually find room to agree with your opponent on this issue if you were to carefully study the development of the internal combustion engine. I wouldn't be surprised if you came away with the view that each component was similarly shaped from some earlier design, much in the same way a modern engine is today.

I don't really care much about arguments like this, however. It's usually nothing more than semantics, and the goal is usually (in my experience) to idealize.
